graphing part 2

Amanda Mae Woodward

2026-11-03

  1. Open the starwars dataset (located in tidyverse)
library(tidyverse)
## ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
## ✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
## ✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
## ✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
## ✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
## ✔ purrr     1.2.2     
## ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
## ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
## ✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
## ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
data(starwars)
  1. Create a scatter plot of character’s height and mass.
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass))+ geom_point()
## Warning: Removed 28 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

2a. Change the color and shape of the points in your scatter plot.

ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass))+ geom_point(color="darkslateblue", shape = 5)
## Warning: Removed 28 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

  1. Add Homeworld as a third variable to your scatterplot.
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, color=homeworld))+ geom_point()
## Warning: Removed 28 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

3a. What do you notice about the graph? (e.g. describe what you see) The legend for homeworlds contains many levels, which makes the graph cluttered and difficult to navigate. The colors are also very similar to one another, making the plot points hard to differentiate.

  1. Make a boxplot of height.
ggplot(starwars, aes(height))+ geom_boxplot()
## Warning: Removed 6 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_boxplot()`).

  1. Make a boxplot of height for each species present in the data.
ggplot(starwars, aes(x= height, y= species))+ geom_boxplot()
## Warning: Removed 6 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_boxplot()`).

5a. change the appearance of your graph in at least 3 ways.

ggplot(starwars, aes(x= height, y= species))+ geom_boxplot(fill = "violet", color= "purple4")+ labs(x= "Height (cm)", y= "Species", title = "Starwars Character Height by Species")+ theme_classic()+ theme(axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 20) )
## Warning: Removed 6 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_boxplot()`).

  1. Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph that uses a color palette from viridis.
library(viridis)
## Loading required package: viridisLite
ggplot(starwars |> filter(!is.na(sex)), aes(height, eye_color, color= sex))+ geom_point(size= 2,)+ scale_color_viridis(option= "viridis", discrete = TRUE)+ labs(x = "Height", y = "Eye Color", color = "Sex", title = "Character Height and Eye Color by Sex")
## Warning: Removed 6 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

7.Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph that uses a color palette from RColorBrewer.

library(RColorBrewer)
ggplot(starwars |> filter(!is.na(hair_color)), aes(x =hair_color, fill = hair_color))+ geom_bar()+ scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3")+ theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))+ labs(x= "Hair Color", y= "Number of Characters", fill= "Hair Color", title = "Frequency of Starwars Character Hair Color")

  1. Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph using facet_wrap
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, color= gender))+ geom_point()+ facet_wrap(~gender)+ labs(x= "Height", y= "Mass", color = "Presenting Gender", title = "Starwars Mass & Height by Presenting Gender")
## Warning: Removed 28 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).
